[Kim (2014)](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1181.pdf) applies word-window convolutions, ReLU and global max-over-time pooling; experimental widths 3/4/5, 100 filters each. Global pooling retains feature presence but discards its location. Missing pretrained words receive random vectors; word embeddings do not inherently share spelling information across rare model numbers. Padding-safe implementation recommendation, rather than a paper claim: for width h, mark windows valid only when all h tokens are nonpadding, mask invalid activations to −∞ before pooling, and return zero when no valid window exists. Zero padding alone is insufficient because convolution biases can create positive padded activations. For short titles, include width 1 so real tokens remain representable; explicitly define larger-width empty outputs.

[Zhang, Zhao and LeCun (2015)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2015/file/250cf8b51c773f3f8dc8b4be867a9a02-Paper.pdf) instead encode characters using a 70-symbol alphabet, processing 1014-character inputs through six convolutions and three fully connected layers. Nonoverlapping local max pools preserve a coarse positional grid before flattening, unlike Kim’s global maximum. This deep architecture should not be copied unchanged for short titles; a shallow character CNN with explicitly defined masks and pooling is an adaptation. Recommendation hypothesis: character filters can share alphanumeric fragments across rare product identifiers, whereas vocabulary truncation to UNK destroys their distinctions. Neither paper establishes recommendation gains or reliable exact-identifier matching; character pooling can also lose distinguishing order or position. A jointly trained character feature encoder inside the single HSTU model could test this hypothesis using permitted metadata, without external pretrained weights.
